rationale: A wins by a hair because it is cleaner on grounding and does not sneak in unsupported assumptions. B has sharper reporter shapes, especially "Bumble says women still message first. Now the AI can write the message," but it overclaims with "it is the first product the returned founder has put their name on" and "the market is trading on the launch." A's "Can a relaunch reverse declining paying users? Bumble bets on AI matchmaking" keeps the missing metric as the story instead of decorating the gap. This is close; both sets are usable, but B has a few too many confident little bridges built over missing facts.
gaps_in_A: "the Dorsey/Schultz/Kalanick-adjacent storyline" is a cute comparator, but Kalanick did not return as CEO, so the reference muddies the founder-return pattern.

"Dating apps add AI to write your opening line" broadens the story to dating apps, but the facts only support Bumble plus unspecified user criticism. A flags this later, but the headline still overreaches.
"Decay: 24hr" on the founder-return angle may be too tight because the return happened earlier this year; the true peg is the relaunch, not the CEO return itself.
gaps_in_B: "it is the first product the returned founder has put their name on since coming back this year" is invented. The update says relaunch under the returning founder-CEO, not first product or personal ownership.
"so the market is trading on the launch, not the result" is an unsupported market claim. The update says stock price fell, not how investors are currently pricing the relaunch.
"Bumble sells subscriptions" is plausible but not supplied. The given fact is declining paying users; don't add business-model shorthand unless the source says it.

"Bumble's founding rule is that women send the first message" is probably true, but the update only says the women-message-first model remains core. For this exercise, that extra historical framing is outside the record.
